A Misunderstanding

Look closely. Think about what each person knows. Create your own story before studying any model.

Task & planning only · No model answer
Your composition task

When things are not what they seem

Write a composition of at least 120 words about a misunderstanding.

The pictures are not arranged in sequence. They are provided to help you think about the topic. Your composition should be based on one or more of these pictures.

Picture A
A damaged bookPicture B
A disagreementPicture C
A note

Consider these points when planning your composition:

  • What was the misunderstanding, and how did it begin?
  • How did the people involved react?
  • How was the misunderstanding cleared up?
  • How did the experience affect the people involved?

You may use the points in any order and include other relevant ideas.

Remember: a misunderstanding involves someone interpreting something incorrectly. Make that mistaken understanding clear in your story.

The minimum length follows the format of your supplied school task. It is not a target for stopping. Develop the important events fully, and follow your teacher’s expectations and your actual time limit.

First look · Before planning

What can you see? What are you assuming?

Observe

Name details that are actually visible in your chosen picture.

Question

What does the picture leave unexplained? Which facts would a character still need to find out?

Choose

Decide which picture or pictures will matter to your story.

You do not have to use all three pictures. You decide the note’s contents and the characters’ roles.

Pause and think

Have an idea of your own?

Explain it aloud in a few sentences. Then open the planning questions to make the story clearer.

The planning questions are hidden. No answers are included.

Develop your own story

Plan the cause, reactions and discovery

Read your plan as a chain: missing information → mistaken belief → reaction → discovery → response. You may arrange the storytelling differently, but the events must still make sense.
Your notebook reminders
  • Keep the same narrative point of view throughout.
  • Place speech marks next to the spoken words and check punctuation around speech tags.
  • Begin a new paragraph when a different person speaks.
  • Use full forms for this practice, following your notebook instruction about contractions.
  • Keep handwriting neat. Move to the next line if a word will not fit.
  • Make the topic clear through the events, not only through the title or final sentence.
